text: An easement gives a nonpossessory right to use another parcel. An express easement ordinarily falls within the statute of frauds and therefore should be memorialized in a signed writing that identifies the servient land and the permitted use.

A claimant establishes adverse possession by proving possession that is actual, open and notorious, exclusive, hostile under the governing claim-of-right standard, and continuous for the statutory period. Permission from the record owner defeats hostility.

Under a race-notice recording statute, a later purchaser prevails only by taking without notice of the earlier interest and recording before the earlier claimant. Inquiry notice may arise from facts that would cause a reasonable buyer to investigate.

A fee simple subject to condition subsequent does not end automatically when the stated condition occurs. The transferor retains a right of entry and must elect to exercise that power before reclaiming possession.

Trespass protects the possessor against intentional physical entry, while private nuisance addresses a substantial and unreasonable interference with use and enjoyment that need not involve entry by a person or object.

The implied warranty of habitability generally requires a residential landlord to maintain premises fit for basic human habitation. A tenant may need to give notice and a reasonable opportunity to repair before invoking statutory or judicial remedies.

Pierson v. Post, 3 Cai. R. 175 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1805), is commonly used to illustrate first possession. This original paraphrase explains that pursuit of a wild animal alone did not create ownership where the pursuer had neither captured nor mortally wounded it.

A classroom problem mentions pursuit, capture, and recording a deed, but asks only whether a museum should catalog a donated fox illustration. It supplies no facts about ownership of land or a living wild animal.

DECISIVE TAIL RULE: A seller who actively conceals a dangerous latent condition cannot rely on caveat emptor; the buyer may seek relief when the defect was undiscoverable by reasonable inspection.

The word notice can describe a meeting announcement, and the word hostile can describe an unfriendly tone. In this linguistic exercise neither term concerns a purchaser, adverse possessor, deed, or land title.
